column2: But in the hall there was left godly Odysseus,
pondering slaughter for the suitors together with Athena;
and at once he addressed Telemachus with winged words:

Telemachus, you must lay away the weapons of war inside,
5	all of them; and the suitors with soft words
6	beguile, when they ask you, missing them:
7	'I have put them away from the smoke, since they are no longer like
8	those which Odysseus once left behind when he went to Troy,
9	but they have been defiled, as far as the breath of fire reached.
10	And besides, this greater thing too a god has cast into my mind:
11	lest somehow, having drunk wine, starting a quarrel among you,
12	you wound one another and disgrace the feast
13	and the wooing; for iron itself draws a man on.'
So he spoke, and Telemachus obeyed his dear father,
and calling out, he said to the nurse Eurycleia:

Nurse, come now, keep the women shut in the halls for me,
17	while I lay away in the chamber my father's gear,
18	the fine things, which in the house neglected the smoke dims,
19	my father being gone; and I was still a child.
20	But now I wish to put them away, where the breath of fire will not reach.
Then his dear nurse Eurycleia spoke to him in turn:

If only, child, you would one day take up good sense
23	to care for the house and guard all the possessions.
24	But come, who then will go with you and bring a light?
25	The maidservants who would give light, you did not let come forward.
Then prudent Telemachus answered her:

This stranger; for I will not suffer one idle who touches
28	my measure of grain, even one who has come from afar.
So he spoke, and her word was wingless.
And she locked the doors of the well-inhabited halls.
And the two, leaping up, Odysseus and his shining son,
carried in the helmets and the bossed shields
and the sharp spears; and before them Pallas Athena,
holding a golden lamp, made a very beautiful light.
Then Telemachus said at once to his father:

O father, truly a great marvel I see with my eyes.
37	Surely the walls of the halls and the fair panels,
38	the fir beams, and the pillars that rise on high
39	appear to my eyes as if of blazing fire.
40	Truly some god is within, of those who hold the broad heaven.
Then answering him spoke Odysseus of many wiles:
So he spoke, and Telemachus went through the hall
to lie down in the chamber, under the blazing torches,
where before he used to sleep, when sweet sleep came upon him;
there then too he lay, and waited for divine Dawn.
But in the hall there was left godly Odysseus,
pondering slaughter for the suitors together with Athena.
And she came out of the chamber, wise Penelope,
like Artemis or golden Aphrodite.
Beside the fire they set a chair for her, where she sat,
inlaid with ivory and silver; which once the craftsman
Icmalius made, and put under it a footstool for the feet,
attached to it, where a great fleece was thrown.
There then sat wise Penelope.
And the white-armed maidservants came from the hall.
They took away much bread and the tables
and the cups from which the overbearing men had drunk;
and the fire from the braziers they threw to the ground, and on them
heaped much other wood, to give light and warmth.
And Melantho rebuked Odysseus a second time:

Stranger, will you still here too be a nuisance through the night,
67	wandering about the house, and spying on the women?
68	But go out of doors, wretch, and be content with your meal;
69	or soon, struck with a brand, you will go out of doors.
Then looking darkly at her spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Strange woman, why do you assail me thus with an angry heart?
72	Is it because I am dirty, and wear bad clothes on my skin,
73	and beg through the district? Necessity presses me.
74	Such are beggars and wandering men.
75	For I too once lived in a house among men,
76	prosperous in a rich house, and often I gave to a wanderer,
77	whatever sort he was and whatever need he came with;
78	and I had slaves very many, and much else
79	by which men live well and are called wealthy.
80	But Zeus the son of Kronos ruined it; for so he wished, I suppose.
81	So now, woman, may you too never lose all
82	the splendour in which you now excel among the maidservants;
83	lest somehow your mistress grow angry and be harsh with you,
84	or Odysseus come; for there is still a portion of hope.
85	But if he has so perished and is no longer to return,
86	yet already there is such a son, by Apollo's will,
87	Telemachus; and none of the women in the halls
88	escapes his notice behaving wantonly, since he is no longer of such an age.
So he spoke, and wise Penelope heard him,
and rebuked the handmaid, and spoke a word and called by name:

Altogether, bold, shameless bitch, you do not escape me
92	doing a great deed, which you shall wipe off on your own head;
93	for you knew all well, since you heard from me myself
94	that I meant to ask the stranger in my halls
95	about my husband, since I am thickly grieved.
She spoke, and said a word to the housekeeper Eurynome:

Eurynome, bring a seat now and a fleece on it,
98	that the stranger may sit and speak a word and listen
99	to me; I wish to question him.
So she spoke, and she very quickly brought and set down
a well-polished seat, and threw a fleece on it;
there then sat the much-enduring godly Odysseus.
And among them wise Penelope began the speaking:

Stranger, this first I myself shall ask you:
105	Who are you among men, and whence? Where is your city and your parents?
Then answering her spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

O woman, no mortal on the boundless earth
108	could find fault with you; for your fame reaches the broad heaven,
109	like that of some blameless king, who god-fearing
110	among many and valiant men rules,
111	upholds good justice, and the black earth bears
112	wheat and barley, and the trees are heavy with fruit,
113	and the flocks bring forth steadily, and the sea supplies fish
114	from his good leading, and the peoples prosper under him.
115	Therefore ask me now of other things in your house,
116	and do not enquire of my race and native land,
117	lest you fill my heart the more with pains
118	as I remember; I am very full of groaning; nor should I
119	sit in another's house wailing and lamenting,
120	since it is worse to grieve unceasingly;
121	lest one of the maidservants blame me, or you yourself,
122	and say I swim in tears, my wits heavy with wine.
Then wise Penelope answered him:

Stranger, my excellence and form and figure
125	the immortals destroyed, when the Argives went up
126	to Ilium, and among them went my husband Odysseus.
127	If he, coming, were to tend my life,
128	greater would be my fame and fairer so.
129	But now I grieve; so many evils has a god heaped on me.
130	For all the best men who hold sway over the islands,
131	Dulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus,
132	and those who dwell around clear-seen Ithaca itself,
133	they woo me against my will, and consume my house.
134	Therefore I pay no heed to strangers, nor to suppliants,
135	nor at all to heralds, who are public workers;
136	but longing for Odysseus I melt away in my heart.
137	They hasten the marriage; but I wind off wiles.
138	A web first a god breathed into my mind,
139	to set up a great loom and weave in the halls
140	a fine and ample cloth; and at once I said to them:
141	'Young men, my suitors, since godly Odysseus is dead,
142	wait, though eager for my marriage, until I finish
143	the cloth—that my threads not perish for nothing—
144	a shroud for the hero Laertes, against the time when
145	the deadly fate of long-lasting death takes him;
146	lest any of the Achaean women in the district blame me,
147	if he lies without a shroud, who had won so much.'
148	So I spoke, and their proud spirit was persuaded.
149	Then by day I would weave the great loom,
150	but at night I would unravel it, when I had set torches by.
151	So for three years I went unnoticed and persuaded the Achaeans;
152	but when the fourth year came and the seasons rolled on,
153	as the months waned, and many days were fulfilled,
154	then through my maidservants, shameless bitches,
155	they came and caught me, and shouted at me with words.
156	So I finished it, and unwillingly, under compulsion.
157	And now I can neither escape marriage nor any other
158	device do I still find; and my parents urge me greatly
159	to marry, and my son is vexed as they eat up his livelihood,
160	knowing it; for he is now a man, one most able
161	to care for a house, to whom Zeus grants glory.
162	But even so tell me your lineage, from where you are.
163	For you are not from the oak of ancient story nor from a rock.
Then answering her spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

O revered wife of Odysseus, son of Laertes,
166	will you not cease asking after my family?
167	But I will tell you; truly you will give me over to griefs
168	more than I am held by; for such is the way, when a man is away
169	from his native land as long a time as I am now,
170	wandering to many cities of mortals, suffering pains;
171	but even so I will tell what you ask and enquire.
172	There is a land called Crete, in the midst of the wine-dark sea,
173	fair and rich, sea-girt; and in it men
174	many, countless, and ninety cities.
175	Language with language is mixed; there are Achaeans,
176	there great-hearted Eteocretans, there Cydonians,
177	and Dorians of waving plumes, and divine Pelasgians.
178	Among them is Cnossus, a great city, where Minos
179	reigned for nine years, familiar of great Zeus,
180	the father of my father, great-hearted Deucalion.
181	And Deucalion begot me and the lord Idomeneus;
182	but he in the beaked ships to Ilium
183	went with the Atreidae; and my famous name is Aethon,
184	younger in birth; and he was older and better.
185	There I saw Odysseus and gave him guest-gifts.
186	For him too the force of the wind brought to Crete,
187	as he was eager for Troy, driving him off course past Malea;
188	and it set him in Amnisus, where is the cave of Eileithyia,
189	in difficult harbours, and he hardly escaped the storms.
190	At once he went up to the town and asked for Idomeneus;
191	for he said he was his guest-friend, dear and honoured.
192	But for him already the tenth or eleventh dawn was
193	since he had gone with the beaked ships to Ilium.
194	Him I led to my house and entertained well,
195	cherishing him heartily, with much in the house;
196	and to his other comrades, who followed with him,
197	from the public store I gave barley-meal and gathered fiery wine
198	and oxen to sacrifice, that they might satisfy their hearts.
199	There for twelve days the godly Achaeans stayed;
200	for the north wind, great, held them, and on the land
201	did not let them stand, some harsh god had roused it.
202	On the thirteenth the wind fell, and they put out.
He made many lies, telling them like truths;
and as she listened, her tears flowed, and her flesh melted;
as snow melts on the high mountains,
which the east wind melts, when the west wind has poured it down;
and as it melts the rivers run full, flowing;
so her fair cheeks melted, as she shed tears,
weeping for her husband, who was sitting beside her. But Odysseus
in his heart pitied his wife as she wept,
but his eyes stood like horn or iron
unmoving in his eyelids; and by craft he hid his tears.
And she, when she had taken her fill of tearful lament,
again answered him and spoke:

Now, stranger, I think I shall test you,
216	whether truly there with godlike comrades
217	you entertained my husband in your halls, as you say.
218	Tell me what sort of clothes he wore on his body,
219	and what sort of man he was himself, and the comrades who followed him.
Then answering her spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

O woman, it is hard, being so long a time apart,
222	to say; for it is now the twentieth year
223	since he went from there and left my country;
224	but I will tell you as my heart pictures it.
225	A purple woolly cloak godly Odysseus had,
226	double; and the brooch for it was made of gold
227	with two sheaths; and in front it was cunningly wrought:
228	with his forepaws a dog held a spotted fawn,
229	gripping it as it struggled; and all marvelled at it,
230	how, though they were gold, the one gripped the fawn throttling it,
231	and the other, eager to escape, struggled with his feet.
232	And the tunic on his body I noticed, shining,
233	like the skin on a dried onion;
234	so soft it was, and bright like the sun;
235	surely many women gazed at him in wonder.
236	And another thing I shall tell you, and lay it to heart:
237	I do not know whether Odysseus wore these on his body from home,
238	or one of his comrades gave them as he boarded the swift ship,
239	or some guest-friend perhaps, since to many Odysseus
240	was dear; for few of the Achaeans were like him.
241	And I gave him a bronze sword and a double cloak,
242	fair, purple, and a fringed tunic,
243	and sent him off with honour onto his well-benched ship.
244	And a herald, a little older than he,
245	followed him; and I will tell you of him too, what sort he was.
246	Round-shouldered, dark-skinned, curly-headed,
247	and Eurybates was his name; and Odysseus honoured him above
248	his other comrades, because he knew what was fitting in his mind.
So he spoke, and in her he roused still more desire for lament,
as she recognised the signs which Odysseus had told her unerringly.
And she, when she had taken her fill of tearful lament,
then answered him and spoke:

Now, stranger, you who before were pitiable to me,
254	in my halls you shall be dear and honoured;
255	for I myself gave these clothes, such as you describe,
256	folding them from the chamber, and put on the shining brooch
257	to be an ornament for him; but I shall not receive him again,
258	come home to his dear native land.
259	So by an evil fate Odysseus in the hollow ship
260	went off to see Ill-Ilium, not to be named.
Then answering her spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

O revered wife of Odysseus, son of Laertes,
263	no longer now spoil your fair skin, nor melt your heart
264	weeping for your husband. Yet I do not blame you at all;
265	for even any woman laments a husband of another kind she has lost,
266	the husband of her youth, to whom she bore children, joined in love,
267	than Odysseus, who they say was like the gods.
268	But cease from lament, and mark my word;
269	for I shall tell you truly and not hide it,
270	how I have already heard of Odysseus' return
271	near, in the rich land of the Thesprotian men,
272	alive; and he brings many good treasures
273	begging through the district. But his trusty comrades
274	he lost, and his hollow ship on the wine-dark sea,
275	coming from the island Thrinacia; for they angered him,
276	Zeus and Helios; for his cattle his comrades killed.
277	They all perished in the much-washed sea;
278	but him on the keel of the ship the wave cast onto the dry land,
279	to the land of the Phaeacians, who are near the gods,
280	who honoured him greatly in their heart like a god
281	and gave him many gifts, and themselves wished to send him
282	home unharmed. And Odysseus would long since have been here;
283	but this seemed to him better in his heart,
284	to gather wealth, going over much land;
285	so far in many gainful devices of mortal men
286	Odysseus knows, nor could any other mortal contend with him.
287	So Pheidon, king of the Thesprotians, told me;
288	and he swore to me himself, pouring a libation in his house,
289	that the ship was launched and the comrades ready,
290	who would send him to his dear native land.
291	But me he sent off first; for a ship chanced to be going
292	of Thesprotian men to wheat-rich Dulichium.
293	And he showed me the possessions, all that Odysseus had gathered;
294	and they would feed another to the tenth generation,
295	such treasures lay in the lord's halls.
296	He said that he had gone to Dodona, to hear from the god's
297	high-leafed oak the counsel of Zeus,
298	how he might return to his dear native land,
299	after being long away, whether openly or in secret.
300	So he is thus safe, and will come soon,
301	very near, and no longer far from friends and native land
302	will he be for long; but all the same I will give you oaths.
303	Let Zeus know first, highest and best of gods,
304	and the hearth of blameless Odysseus, to which I have come,
305	that all this will be accomplished as I say.
306	In this very year Odysseus will come here,
307	as this month wanes, and the next begins.
Then wise Penelope spoke to him in turn:

Would that, stranger, this word might be fulfilled;
310	then you would soon know friendship and many gifts
311	from me, so that anyone meeting you would call you blessed.
312	But thus it is in my heart, as it will be:
313	neither will Odysseus come home again, nor will you
314	get a convoy, since there are not such masters in the house
315	as Odysseus was among men, if ever he was,
316	to send off honoured strangers and to receive them.
317	But, handmaids, wash him, and spread a bed,
318	bedding and cloaks and shining rugs,
319	that warm and well he may reach golden-throned Dawn.
320	And at very early dawn wash him and anoint him,
321	that inside beside Telemachus he may take thought for his dinner
322	sitting in the hall; and the worse for whichever of them
323	vexes him, heart-destroying; he shall accomplish nothing
324	here any more, however terribly angered.
325	For how, stranger, will you learn about me, whether in anything
326	I surpass other women in mind and prudent counsel,
327	if unwashed, clad in bad clothes in the halls
328	you feast? Men are short-lived.
329	Whoever is himself harsh and knows harshness,
330	on him all mortals call down woes hereafter
331	while he lives, and when he is dead all mock him;
332	but whoever is himself blameless and knows blamelessness,
333	his wide fame strangers carry
334	to all men, and many call him good.
Then answering her spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

O revered wife of Odysseus, son of Laertes,
337	cloaks and shining rugs were hateful to me,
338	from the time I first left the snowy mountains of Crete
339	going on a long-oared ship,
340	but I shall lie as before I used to lie sleepless nights;
341	for many nights on a mean bed
342	I lay and waited for fair-throned divine Dawn.
343	And foot-baths do not please my heart at all;
344	nor shall a woman touch my foot
345	of those who are servants in your house,
346	unless there is some old woman, ancient, who knows kindly things,
347	who has suffered as much in her mind as I have;
348	I would not begrudge her touching my feet.
Then wise Penelope spoke to him in turn:

Dear stranger; for no prudent man yet so
351	of far-off dear strangers has come to my house,
352	as you speak all things so clearly and prudently.
353	I have an old woman, with careful thoughts in her mind,
354	who nursed that ill-fated man well and tended him,
355	taking him in her hands, when first his mother bore him;
356	she will wash your feet, though she is weak.
357	But come now, rise, wise Eurycleia,
358	wash one of the same age as your master; and perhaps Odysseus
359	is already such in his feet and such in his hands;
360	for quickly in misfortune mortals grow old.
So she spoke, and the old woman covered her face with her hands,
and shed hot tears, and spoke a word of lament:

Ah me, child, helpless for you; surely above all men Zeus
364	hated you, who have a god-fearing heart.
365	For no mortal ever burned to thunder-delighting Zeus
366	so many fat thigh-pieces nor choice hecatombs
367	as you gave him, praying that you might reach
368	a sleek old age and rear a shining son;
369	but now from you alone he has utterly taken away the day of return.
370	So perhaps also him the women mocked
371	of far-off strangers, whenever he came to some famous house,
372	as these bitches all mock you,
373	whose insult and many shames you avoid
374	and do not let them wash you; and me, not unwilling, she bade,
375	the daughter of Icarius, wise Penelope.
376	Therefore I will wash your feet, both for Penelope herself
377	and for you, since my heart within is stirred
378	with sorrows. But come now, understand the word I shall say:
379	many long-suffering strangers have come here,
380	but I say I have never yet seen anyone so like
381	as you are like Odysseus in figure, voice and feet.
Then answering her spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

Old woman, so say all who have seen with their eyes
384	the two of us, that we are very like each other,
385	as you yourself, thinking, say.
So he spoke, and the old woman took the shining basin
with which she washed his feet, and poured in much water,
cold, and then poured in the warm. But Odysseus
sat by the hearth, and quickly turned to the dark;
for at once he felt in his heart, lest, taking him,
she might notice the scar and the deeds be made open.
She came near and washed her lord; and at once she knew
the scar, which once a boar struck him with a white tusk
when he went to Parnassus to Autolycus and his sons,
his mother's noble father, who surpassed men
in thievery and oath; and a god himself gave it to him,
Hermes; for to him he burned pleasing thigh-pieces
of lambs and kids; and he followed him with ready goodwill.
And Autolycus, coming to the rich land of Ithaca,
found the newly born child of his daughter;
him Eurycleia set on his knees
as he finished supper, and spoke a word and called by name:

Autolycus, find now yourself a name to give
404	your daughter's dear child; much prayed for is he to you.
Then Autolycus answered her and spoke:

My son-in-law and daughter, give the name I shall say;
407	for I come here having been angry with many,
408	men and women over the much-nourishing earth;
409	so let Odysseus be the name given to him; and I,
410	whenever he has grown up and comes to his mother's great house
411	at Parnassus, where my possessions are,
412	of these I shall give him and send him off rejoicing.
For these things Odysseus went, that he might give him splendid gifts.
Him Autolycus and the sons of Autolycus
welcomed with hands and honeyed words;
and his mother's mother Amphithea, clasping Odysseus,
kissed him on the head and both his fair eyes.
And Autolycus called to his glorious sons
to prepare a dinner; and they heard him urging,
and at once brought in a male ox of five years;
they flayed it and dressed it, and cut it all up,
and chopped it skilfully and pierced it on spits,
and roasted it carefully, and divided the portions.
So then for the whole day till the sun set
they feasted, and their spirit lacked nothing of the equal feast;
and when the sun set and darkness came,
then they lay down and took the gift of sleep.
And when early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
they went off to the hunt, both the dogs and the sons
of Autolycus themselves; and among them godly Odysseus
went; and they climbed the steep mountain clothed in woods,
of Parnassus, and soon reached the windy folds.
The sun was just striking the fields,
rising from the gently flowing, deep-streaming Oceanus,
and the beaters came to a glen; and before them
the dogs went tracking the trail, and behind
the sons of Autolycus; and among them godly Odysseus
went near the dogs, brandishing a long-shadowed spear.
There in a thick lair lay a great boar;
through it neither the force of the wet-blowing winds went,
nor did the shining sun strike it with his rays,
nor did the rain pass through; so thick it was,
and of leaves there was a huge heap within.
And the noise of men and dogs and their feet came about it,
as they came on in pursuit; and it, facing them from the thicket,
bristling its crest well, with fire in its eyes as it glared,
stood close to them; and Odysseus first
rushed, holding up the long spear in his stout hand,
eager to strike; but the boar, anticipating, struck him
above the knee, and tore much flesh with its tusk,
charging sidelong, but did not reach the man's bone.
And Odysseus struck it, hitting it on the right shoulder,
and straight through went the point of the shining spear;
and it fell in the dust, bellowing, and its life flew away.
Him the dear sons of Autolycus busied themselves about,
and the wound of blameless godlike Odysseus
they bound skilfully, and with a charm they stopped the dark blood,
and quickly came to the house of their dear father.
Him Autolycus and the sons of Autolycus,
having healed him well and given splendid gifts,
quickly sent rejoicing to his dear native land,
to Ithaca. His father and lady mother
rejoiced at his return and asked about each thing,
about the scar, how he got it; and he told them well
how, as he hunted, a boar struck him with a white tusk,
when he went to Parnassus with the sons of Autolycus.
This scar the old woman, taking it in the flat of her hands,
recognised by feeling, and let the foot fall;
his leg fell into the basin, and the bronze rang,
and tilted to the other side; and the water spilled on the ground.
Joy and grief together seized her heart, and her two eyes
filled with tears, and her lusty voice was stopped.
And touching Odysseus' chin she said to him:

Truly you are Odysseus, dear child; and I did not
475	know you before, until I had touched all my master.
She spoke, and looked with her eyes at Penelope,
wishing to tell her that her dear husband was within.
But she could not look straight at her nor perceive;
for Athena had turned her mind aside; but Odysseus,
feeling for her throat, seized it with his right hand,
and with the other drew her nearer to him and spoke:

Nurse, why do you wish to destroy me? You yourself nursed me
483	at your own breast; and now, having suffered many pains,
484	I have come in the twentieth year to my native land.
485	But since you have perceived it and a god has put it in your mind,
486	be silent, lest anyone else in the halls learn it.
487	For thus I will say, and it shall indeed be accomplished:
488	if a god by my hand subdues the noble suitors,
489	I shall not spare you, though you are my nurse, when I kill
490	the other women, the maidservants, in my halls.
Then wise Eurycleia spoke to him in turn:

My child, what word has escaped the fence of your teeth!
493	You know how steadfast and unyielding my strength is,
494	and I shall hold out like hard stone or iron.
495	And another thing I shall tell you, and lay it in your mind:
496	if a god by your hand subdues the noble suitors,
497	then I shall list for you the women in the halls,
498	those who dishonour you and those who are blameless.
Then answering her spoke Odysseus of many wiles:
So he spoke, and the old woman went through the hall
to fetch water for the foot-bath; for the first was all spilled.
But when she had washed him and anointed him richly with oil,
again Odysseus drew his chair nearer to the fire
to warm himself, and covered the scar with his rags.
And among them wise Penelope began the speaking:

Stranger, this little thing I shall ask you myself:
510	for soon will be the hour of sweet rest,
511	for whomever sweet sleep takes, even one in sorrow.
512	But to me a god has given even measureless grief;
513	for by day I take pleasure in mourning, lamenting,
514	looking to my own works and those of the handmaids in the house;
515	but when night comes, and sleep takes all,
516	I lie on my bed, and thick sharp cares
517	around my throbbing heart torment me as I mourn.
518	As when the daughter of Pandareus, the greenish nightingale,
519	sings beautifully when spring has newly begun,
520	sitting in the thick leaves of the trees,
521	and often changing, pours forth her many-sounding voice,
522	lamenting her child Itylus, dear, whom once with the bronze
523	she killed in folly, the son of lord Zethus;
524	so too my heart is stirred this way and that,
525	whether to stay with my son and keep everything safe,
526	my property, my maidservants and the great high-roofed house,
527	respecting my husband's bed and the people's talk,
528	or to follow now whichever of the Achaeans is best
529	who woos me in the halls, bringing countless wooing-gifts.
530	While my son was still a child and light of mind,
531	he did not allow me to marry and leave my husband's house;
532	but now that he is big and has reached the measure of youth,
533	he even prays that I go away from the hall,
534	vexed for his property, which the Achaeans eat up.
535	But come, interpret this dream for me, and listen.
536	Twenty geese in the house eat wheat
537	from the water, and I rejoice looking at them;
538	but a great eagle with crooked beak came down from the mountain
539	and broke the necks of all and killed them; and they lay poured out
540	in a heap in the halls, and he was lifted up into the bright air.
541	But I wept and wailed, in a dream though it was,
542	and round me gathered the fair-tressed Achaean women,
543	as I piteously lamented that the eagle had killed my geese.
544	And coming back he sat on a projecting beam of the roof,
545	and with human voice he restrained me and spoke:
546	'Be of good courage, daughter of far-famed Icarius;
547	this is no dream but a waking good, which shall be accomplished for you.
548	The geese are the suitors, and I, who was before the eagle,
549	a bird, now have come again as your husband,
550	who shall let loose on all the suitors a shameful doom.'
551	So he spoke, and honey-sweet sleep released me;
552	and looking about I saw the geese in the halls
553	eating wheat from the trough, where they were before.
Then answering her spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

O woman, it is in no way possible to interpret the dream
556	turning it aside to another meaning, since Odysseus himself
557	has told you how he will fulfil it; destruction is shown for the suitors,
558	for all of them, and none will escape death and the fates.
Then wise Penelope spoke to him in turn:

Stranger, dreams are hard to deal with, with unclear speech,
561	and not everything in them is fulfilled for men.
562	For there are two gates of shadowy dreams;
563	one is made of horn, the other of ivory;
564	those that come through the sawn ivory
565	deceive, bringing words that are unaccomplished;
566	but those that come out through the polished horn
567	bring true things to pass, when any mortal sees them.
568	But I do not think that from here the dread dream
569	came; it would indeed be welcome to me and my son.
570	And another thing I shall tell you, and lay it in your mind:
571	this dawn is coming, ill-named, which will part me from Odysseus'
572	house; for now I shall set up a contest,
573	the axes, which he in his halls
574	used to set up in a row, like ship's props, twelve in all;
575	and standing far off he would shoot an arrow through.
576	Now I shall set this contest to the suitors;
577	whoever most easily strings the bow in his hands
578	and shoots an arrow through all twelve axes,
579	with him I shall go, leaving this house,
580	my wedded home, very beautiful, full of livelihood;
581	which I think I shall remember even in a dream.
Then answering her spoke Odysseus of many wiles:

O revered wife of Odysseus, son of Laertes,
584	no longer put off this contest in the house;
585	for before them Odysseus of many wiles will come here,
586	before these men, handling this well-polished bow,
587	string the cord and shoot through the iron.
Then wise Penelope spoke to him in turn:

If you were willing, stranger, to sit beside me in the halls
590	and delight me, sleep would not be poured on my eyelids.
591	But it is not possible for men to be always sleepless;
592	for the immortals have set a portion for each
593	for mortals on the grain-giving earth.
594	But I, going up to the upper chamber,
595	shall lie on my bed, which has been made for me a place of groaning,
596	always stained with my tears, since Odysseus
597	went off to see Ill-Ilium, not to be named.
598	There I shall lie down; and you lie down in this house,
599	either spreading a bed on the ground, or let them lay out bedding.
So saying she went up to the shining upper chamber,
not alone; with her went the other handmaids too.
And having gone up to the upper chamber with her women attendants
she then wept for Odysseus, her dear husband, till on her
grey-eyed Athena cast sweet sleep on her eyelids.
